[[File:SQMSept2011Day4.jpg|thumb|Johann Rafelski lecturing at the International Conference on Strangeness in Quark Matter in 2011.]]
'''Johann Rafelski''' (born 19 May 1950) is a German-American theoretical physicist. He is a professor of physics at the [[University of Arizona]] in [[Tucson]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://facultygovernance.arizona.edu/faculty-senate/roster|title=Faculty Senate roster|website=The University of Arizona|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191204234450/https://facultygovernance.arizona.edu/faculty-senate/roster|archive-date=4 December 2019|access-date=10 March 2020}}</ref> guest scientist at [[CERN]] ([[Geneva]]),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://inspirehep.net/search?&f=recid|title=Rafelski's scientific articles published with CERN affiliation|date=10 March 2020|website=INSPIRE HEP database}}</ref> and has been LMU-Excellent Guest Professor at [[LMU Munich]] in Germany.

Rafelski's current research interests center around investigation of the vacuum structure of [[quantum chromodynamics]] (QCD) and [[quantum electrodynamics]] (QED) in the presence of strong fields; study of the QCD vacuum structure and deconfinement with strange particle production<ref name="RafelskiMüller1986">{{cite journal|last1=Rafelski|first1=Johann|last2=Müller|first2=Berndt|title=Strangeness Production in the Quark–Gluon Plasma|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=56|issue=21|year=1986|pages=2334|issn=0031-9007|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.56.2334|doi-access=free}}</ref> in deconfined [[quark–gluon plasma]] formed in relativistic heavy ion collisions; the formation of matter out of quark–gluon plasma in the [[hadronization]] process,<ref name="KochMüller1986">{{cite journal|last1=Koch|first1=P|last2=Müller|first2=B|last3=Rafelski|first3=J|title=Strangeness in relativistic heavy ion collisions|journal=Physics Reports|volume=142|issue=4|year=1986|pages=167–262|issn=0370-1573|doi=10.1016/0370-1573(86)90096-7|bibcode=1986PhR...142..167K|citeseerx=10.1.1.462.8703}}</ref> also in the [[Big Bang|early Universe]];<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Fromerth|first1=Michael J.|last2=Rafelski|first2=Johann|date=2003-04-15|title=Hadronization of the Quark Universe|eprint=astro-ph/0211346}}</ref> considering antimatter formation and annihilation. He has also contributed to the physics of table top muon-catalyzed fusion<ref name="RafelskiJones1987">{{cite journal|last1=Rafelski|first1=Johann|last2=Jones|first2=Steven E.|year=1987|title=Cold Nuclear Fusion|jstor=24979424|journal=Scientific American|volume=257|issue=1|pages=84–89|doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0787-84|bibcode=1987SciAm.257a..84R|issn=0036-8733}}</ref> and the ascent of ultrashort laser light pulses<ref name="Cowen2013">{{cite journal|last1=Cowen|first1=Ron|year=2013|title=Two-laser boron fusion lights the way to radiation-free energy|journal=Nature|doi=10.1038/nature.2013.13914|s2cid=137981473|issn=0028-0836}}</ref> as a new tool in this domain of physics. He contributed to understanding of neural nets and artificial intelligence<ref name="ClarkRafelski1985">{{cite journal|last1=Clark|first1=John W.|last2=Rafelski|first2=Johann|last3=Winston|first3=Jeffrey V.|year=1985|title=Brain without mind: Computer simulation of neural networks with modifiable neuronal interactions|journal=Physics Reports|volume=123|issue=4|pages=215–273|doi=10.1016/0370-1573(85)90038-9|bibcode=1985PhR...123..215C|issn=0370-1573}}</ref> showing importance of neural plasticity and "sleep".

==Career==
Rafelski studied physics at [[Goethe University Frankfurt]] in [[Germany]], where he received his [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in the spring of 1973 working with [[Walter Greiner]] on strong fields<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rafelski|first1=J.|last2=Müller|first2=B.|last3=Greiner|first3=W.|year=1974|title=The charged vacuum in over-critical fields|journal=Nuclear Physics B|volume=68|issue=2|pages=585–604|doi=10.1016/0550-3213(74)90333-2|bibcode=1974NuPhB..68..585R}}</ref> and muonic atom tests of QED.<ref>{{Cite thesis|type=PhD|last=Rafelski|first=Johann|title=Selbstkonsistente Vielteilchengleichungen fur Elektronen und Muonen und ihre Effekte in Muonischen Atomen|publisher=Frankfurt University|year=1973|url=https://inspirehep.net/record/1468116/files/Thesis-1973-Rafelski.pdf|location=Frankfurt}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rafelski|first1=Johann|last2=Müller|first2=Berndt|last3=Soff|first3=Gerhard|last4=Greiner|first4=Walter|year=1974|title=Critical discussion of the vacuum polarization measurements in muonic atoms|journal=Annals of Physics|volume=88|issue=2|pages=419–453|doi=10.1016/0003-4916(74)90177-8|bibcode=1974AnPhy..88..419R}}</ref> In 1973, he began a series of [[postdoctoral fellowship]]s: first at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] ([[Philadelphia]]) with [[Abraham Klein (physicist)|Abraham Klein]], then at the [[Argonne National Laboratory]] near [[Chicago]] where he worked with [[John Walter Clark|John W. Clark]] of [[Washington University in St. Louis]] and Michael Danos<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.lib.uchicago.edu/e/scrc/findingaids/view.php?eadid=ICU.SPCL.MDANOS|title=Guide to the Michael Danos Papers 1950-2003|website=lib.uchicago.edu|access-date=2020-03-17|quote=Box 22, folder 8: Rafelski, biographical material and letters of recommendation, 1991}}</ref><ref name="Danos2001">{{cite book|author=Michael Danos|title=Proceedings of the Symposium on Fundamental Issues in Elementary Matter: 25-29 September 2000, Bad Honnef, Germany : in honor and memory of Michael Danos|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aOsWAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA416|year=2001|publisher=EP Systema|isbn=978-963-00-5764-6|pages=416–}}</ref> of National Bureau of Standards (now [[National Institute of Standards and Technology|NIST]]).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1999-09-03-9909030207-story.html|title=Theoretical physicist Michael Danos|last=O'Brien|first=Margaret|date=3 Sep 1999|website=Chicago Tribune|access-date=2020-03-17}}</ref> In the spring of 1977, Rafelski moved for a few months to work at the [[Gesellschaft für Schwerionenforschung|GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research]] in Germany, then continued on to a fellowship at CERN<ref>{{cite journal|title=The Authors|journal=Scientific American|volume=241|issue=6|year=1979|pages=19|issn=0036-8733|doi=10.1038/scientificamerican1279-19|bibcode=1979SciAm.241f..19.}}</ref> where he worked with [[Rolf Hagedorn]] and [[John Stewart Bell|John S. Bell]]; Rafelski remains associated with CERN to this day.<ref name="Rafelski2020">{{cite journal|last1=Rafelski|first1=Johann|title=Discovery of Quark–Gluon Plasma: Strangeness Diaries|journal=The European Physical Journal Special Topics|volume=229|issue=1|year=2020|pages=1–140|issn=1951-6355|doi=10.1140/epjst/e2019-900263-x|arxiv=1911.00831|bibcode=2020EPJST.229....1R|s2cid=207869782}}</ref>

In the fall of 1979, Rafelski was appointed tenured associate professor at Goethe University Frankfurt where he taught for 4 years, while collaborating closely with Hagedorn, [[Berndt Müller]] and [[:de:Gerhard Soff|Gerhard Soff]], whom Rafelski mentored in his PhD work. Rafelski then accepted the chair of Theoretical Physics at the [[University of Cape Town]] (South Africa)<ref>{{Cite book|last=Rafelski|first=Johann|url=https://inspirehep.net/record/1750535/files/Rafelski.pdf|title=Why and how in theoretical physics : inaugural lecture|publisher=University of Cape Town|year=1984|isbn=9780799205886|location=Cape Town}}</ref> where he created a Theoretical Physics and Astrophysics Institute before moving to The University of Arizona in the fall of 1987. During these years he was also a guest scientist at NIST in [[Washington, D.C.]] His interests in muon-catalyzed fusion and other table-top fusion methods led him to a collaboration led by [[Steven E. Jones]]<ref>{{cite journal|title=The Authors|journal=Scientific American|volume=257|issue=1|year=1987|pages=14–15|issn=0036-8733|doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0787-14|bibcode=1987SciAm.257a..14.}}</ref> working at the [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]].<ref name="JonesPalmer1989">{{cite journal|last1=Jones|first1=S. E.|last2=Palmer|first2=E. P.|last3=Czirr|first3=J. B.|last4=Decker|first4=D. L.|last5=Jensen|first5=G. L.|last6=Thorne|first6=J. M.|last7=Taylor|first7=S. F.|last8=Rafelski|first8=J.|title=Observation of cold nuclear fusion in condensed matter|journal=Nature|volume=338|issue=6218|year=1989|pages=737–740|issn=0028-0836|doi=10.1038/338737a0|bibcode=1989Natur.338..737J|s2cid=40352698}}</ref> The start-up of experimental work on quark–gluon plasma has led to another enduring collaboration with the [[Paris Diderot University|University of Paris 7-Jussieu]] involving Jean Letessier.<ref name="RafelskiLetessier2004">{{cite journal|last1=Rafelski|first1=Johann|last2=Letessier|first2=Jean|title=Strangeness and quark–gluon plasma|journal=Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics|volume=30|issue=1|year=2004|pages=S1–S28|issn=0954-3899|doi=10.1088/0954-3899/30/1/001|arxiv=hep-ph/0305284|bibcode=2004JPhG...30S...1R|s2cid=119326264}}</ref>

Rafelski has remained involved in the study of [[quark–gluon plasma]] (QGP) and advancing [[strangeness production]] as the pivotal QGP signature,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Quercigh|first1=Emanuele|last2=Rafelski|first2=Johann|year=2000|title=A strange quark plasma|journal=Physics World|volume=13|issue=10|pages=37–42|doi=10.1088/2058-7058/13/10/35|s2cid=125674588 |issn=0953-8585|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/715770}}</ref><ref name="Rafelski2020" /> for which the first experimental evidence was announced by [[CERN]] in February 2000<ref name="Abbott2000">{{cite journal|last1=Abbott|first1=Alison|title=CERN claims first experimental creation of quark–gluon plasma|journal=Nature|volume=403|issue=6770|year=2000|pages=581|issn=0028-0836|doi=10.1038/35001196|pmid=10688162|bibcode=2000Natur.403..581A|doi-access=free}}</ref> and which has now become a new field of physics.<ref name="Torrieri2012">{{cite journal|last1=Torrieri|first1=G.|title=My Strange Times with Johann Rafelski|journal=Acta Physica Polonica B|volume=43|issue=4|year=2012|pages=821|issn=0587-4254|doi=10.5506/APhysPolB.43.821|s2cid=119195994|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2020/01/200131114737.htm|title=Exploring strangeness and the primordial Universe|date=31 January 2020|work=ScienceDaily|access-date=12 March 2020}}</ref><ref name="Rafelski2020" /> This work relates to his long-lasting studies of the structured quantum vacuum,<ref name="FulcherRafelski1979">{{cite journal|last1=Fulcher|first1=Lewis P.|last2=Rafelski|first2=Johann|last3=Klein|first3=Abraham|year=1979|title=The Decay of the Vacuum|jstor=24965361|journal=Scientific American|volume=241|issue=6|pages=150–159|doi=10.1038/scientificamerican1279-150|bibcode=1979SciAm.241f.150F|issn=0036-8733}}</ref> also known as [[Lorentz ether theory|Lorentz Invariant Aether]].

== ''Melting Hadrons, Boiling Quarks'' ==
''[[Melting Hadrons, Boiling Quarks]]'' is a scientific book series edited by Rafelski.<ref name="MHBQ">{{Cite book|title=Melting Hadrons, Boiling Quarks - From Hagedorn Temperature to Ultra-Relativistic Heavy-Ion Collisions at CERN|date=2016|publisher=Springer International Publishing|isbn=978-3-319-17544-7|editor-last=Rafelski|editor-first=Johann|location=Cham|bibcode=2016mhbq.book.....R|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-17545-4}}</ref> The first volume of 2016 published as [[Open-access monograph|open-access]] under the [[Creative Commons license]] 4.0.<ref>{{Cite web|title=eBooks for all!|url=https://home.cern/news/announcement/cern/ebooks-all|access-date=2020-07-13|website=CERN}}</ref> is subtitled 'From Hagedorn Temperature to ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions at CERN', and the volume in preparation was subtitled '[[Quark–gluon plasma]] discovery at CERN'. In the foreword of the first volume, former director-general of [[CERN]] [[Herwig Schopper]] states that the book fulfills two purposes which have been neglected for a long time.<ref name="MHBQ"/> Primarily a ''[[festschrift]]'' (an 'honorary book'), it "...delivers the proper credit to physicist [[Rolf Hagedorn]] for his important role at the birth of a new research field"; and it describes how a development which he started just 50 years ago is "...closely connected to the most recent surprises in the new experimental domain of relativistic heavy ion physics...".<ref name="MHBQ"/>

Évi: Rendes, levelező, külső és tiszteleti tagok |publisher=Magyar Tudományos Akadémia |year=2022 |location=Budapest |pages=151 (pdf, no printed pagination) |language=hu}}</ref>

==Private life==
Rafelski was born in [[Kraków]], Poland, on May 19, 1950. In 1973 Rafelski married Helga Betz, with whom he had two children. Dr. Helga Rafelski died of cancer in 2000. In 2003 Rafelski married the American novelist Victoria Grossack.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Pufeles families|url=https://www.ics.uci.edu/~dan/genealogy/Krakow/Families/Pufeles.html|access-date=2021-04-01|website=ics.uci.edu}}</ref>
